profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
authoring_note: Original content informed by the public framework structure and role-profile intent. No Jisc descriptor text is reproduced or closely paraphrased.

framework_structure_informed_by: Jisc BDC six-element structure and role-profile architecture
source_strategy.role_lens: Generic profile for any learner or member of staff.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Keeps essential digital tasks moving but still relies on prompts, familiar routines or local help when work becomes less predictable.
observable_practices: Uses calendar and task tools for routine everyday work or study when a known example or clear instructions are available.
Keeps shared file spaces moving with some structure, but consistency drops when the task becomes unfamiliar or time-pressured.
Can recover from minor issues in core productivity apps through search, help or local support, although interruptions still slow progress.
evidence_examples: Examples showing routine use of calendar and task tools for predictable tasks.
A simple file, checklist or message trail in shared file spaces that shows work can be completed, albeit with some friction.
A support request, self-note or reflection describing how an issue in core productivity apps was resolved.

common_misconceptions.claim: Owning or accessing many apps means the basics are secure.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Breadth of access can hide fragile workflow habits and version confusion.

common_misconceptions.claim: Getting through the task once shows the process is reliable.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: One-off success does not show independent, repeatable practice.

Enough orientation or support to attempt routine tasks safely.

Progress is easier when Digital Identity and Wellbeing is at least emerging alongside this element.
entries.respondent_visibility: Best judged by the individual plus close collaborators who see everyday workflow habits and reliability.
progression_signals: Moves from scattered personal workarounds to a repeatable setup.
Handles common issues with less interruption.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Uses core tools independently, chooses sensible workflows and solves common issues without much interruption.
observable_practices: Uses calendar and task tools independently and chooses sensible settings or features for the job rather than relying on default habits.
Organises shared file spaces so that current materials, deadlines and permissions are easier for other people to follow.
Troubleshoots common problems in core productivity apps and makes practical choices that reduce avoidable friction.
evidence_examples: A clean, consistently used setup in calendar and task tools that other people can navigate without extra explanation.
A short process note, template or annotated example from shared file spaces showing independent workflow choices.
A troubleshooting example from core productivity apps where the person diagnosed and fixed a common problem.

common_misconceptions.claim: Being quick personally is the same as having a good workflow.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: A strong personal workaround may still be opaque or awkward for others.

common_misconceptions.claim: A preferred tool is automatically the right choice everywhere.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Fit depends on context, interoperability, support and inclusion.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Optimises workflows, judges tool choices critically and improves practice for other people as well as for themselves.
observable_practices: Improves calendar and task tools so that reliability, accessibility or efficiency increase for a wider group, not just for personal use.
Reviews shared file spaces critically, removing duplication and simplifying the workflow where needed.
Makes well-judged decisions about core productivity apps with attention to interoperability, support burden, inclusion and risk.
evidence_examples: A redesigned or simplified approach to calendar and task tools adopted by others or endorsed locally.
Before-and-after evidence from shared file spaces showing improved reliability, accessibility or efficiency.
A comparison or rationale for choices in core productivity apps that weighs fit, risk, support and interoperability.

common_misconceptions.claim: Proficiency means always adopting the newest or most advanced platform.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Judgment and simplification often matter more than feature depth.

common_misconceptions.claim: If a process works for experts it should work for everyone.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Sustainable improvement must account for different users, needs and support conditions.

observable_practices: Adapts existing digital resources for immediate use, but most choices still follow familiar patterns rather than an explicit design rationale.
Uses workflow fixes to solve a local problem once the route is reasonably clear.
Experiments with templates or prototypes in a limited way, though evaluation is still mainly about whether something worked at all.

common_misconceptions.claim: Trying a new tool is enough evidence of creative capability.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Capability lies in the problem solved and the design decisions made.

Uses workflow fixes to remove repeated effort or improve clarity, consistency or accessibility.

common_misconceptions.claim: More interactivity always means better design.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Good design serves the need; extra features can add friction.

entries.capability_statement: Designs reusable, evaluative and innovative solutions that improve practice beyond the immediate task.
observable_practices: Creates digital resources that other people can reuse, adapt or scale with minimal extra explanation.
Treats workflow fixes as part of an improvement cycle, with feedback and evidence informing later iterations.
Uses templates or prototypes to support original, well-scoped innovation rather than novelty for its own sake.

common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Proficient practice keeps learning from use, context change and feedback.

entries.capability_statement: Learns reactively when a new need appears and often stops once the immediate task is complete.
observable_practices: Uses short courses and guides when a new need arises, but development activity is still mostly reactive and short-term.
Tries out ideas from practice experiments in isolated moments without always checking what changed in practice.
Joins peer learning exchanges when prompted or when confidence is low, though follow-through may be limited once the pressure passes.
evidence_examples: Completion of short courses and guides linked to an immediate need.
A brief example of trying something from practice experiments once or twice in practice.
Participation records or notes from peer learning exchanges with limited follow-through.

common_misconceptions.claim: Watching training content is the same as improving practice.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Development is visible only when learning is applied and reflected on.

common_misconceptions.claim: Only formal courses count as digital development.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Practice, peer exchange and experimentation also matter.

entries.capability_statement: Finds usable sources or data for immediate tasks, but evaluation of quality, limitations and relevance is still inconsistent.
observable_practices: Uses searches and source collections to locate material for immediate tasks, but source quality checks are still inconsistent.
Reads spreadsheets or dashboards with some care, though assumptions, gaps or definitions can still be missed.
Draws on briefs or summaries to support decisions, but confidence is sometimes based more on convenience than on evidence strength.
evidence_examples: A saved set of searches and source collections used to complete an immediate task.
A worked example using spreadsheets or dashboards with some attention to meaning, though not all assumptions are checked.
A note or draft using briefs or summaries that shows a plausible but still limited evidence base.

common_misconceptions.claim: A source is reliable if it appears high in search results or looks professional.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Presentation and ranking do not guarantee trustworthiness or fit.

common_misconceptions.claim: Numbers speak for themselves.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Data always depends on definitions, omissions, context and interpretation.

Interprets spreadsheets or dashboards with attention to definitions, missing information, timeframe and context.
Uses briefs or summaries to make reasoned judgments and can explain the limits of the evidence.
evidence_examples: An evidence trail from searches and source collections showing source comparison and selection criteria.
An annotated interpretation of spreadsheets or dashboards that explains caveats, definitions or missing data.
A decision note using briefs or summaries that distinguishes stronger from weaker evidence.

common_misconceptions.claim: Rejecting biased sources is the same as critical literacy.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Critical literacy often requires weighing imperfect evidence, not just discarding it.

common_misconceptions.claim: A neat dashboard is automatically decision-ready.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Visual clarity can conceal weak measures, missing data or poor alignment with the question.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Facilitates productive collaboration or community participation and shapes better digital communication norms.
observable_practices: Designs or facilitates email or messaging channels so that collaboration is clearer, more balanced and more resilient.
Uses shared workspaces to support collective decision-making, accountability and participation across different needs.
Shapes communities or project spaces by modelling good norms, managing tension early and helping others contribute well.
evidence_examples: A facilitated structure for email or messaging channels that improved collaboration quality or inclusion.
Records from shared workspaces showing balanced participation, decision clarity and follow-through.
Examples from communities or project spaces where norms were shaped deliberately and conflict or exclusion was handled well.

common_misconceptions.claim: Facilitation means posting most often.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Good facilitators create space for others and guide participation deliberately.

common_misconceptions.claim: If conflict is visible, collaboration has failed.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Handled well, tension can improve clarity and decision quality.

Enough scope to review, improve or influence practice beyond immediate personal use.

Progress is easier when Digital Learning and Development is at least emerging alongside this element.
Progress is easier when Digital Identity and Wellbeing is at least emerging alongside this element.
entries.respondent_visibility: Visible to collaborators, learners, service users or community members who experience the communication pattern.
progression_signals: Shapes healthier communication norms in communities.
Manages tension and participation with confidence and care.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Responds to digital identity or wellbeing issues after they arise, with actions that are often platform-specific or temporary.
observable_practices: Adjusts profiles and privacy settings after an issue appears, though the response is often temporary or limited to one platform.
Manages notification patterns inconsistently, leading to cycles of overload, distraction or blurred boundaries.
Responds to community norms when prompted, but does not yet maintain a deliberate long-term approach.
evidence_examples: A reactive change to profiles and privacy settings after a concern or incident.
Short-term use of notification patterns to reduce overload or distraction.
A note or reflection about community norms that identifies a risk but has not yet become a stable practice.

common_misconceptions.claim: Changing one privacy setting solves digital identity risk.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Presence, boundaries and context usually span several platforms and practices.

common_misconceptions.claim: Overload is just a personal time-management issue.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Digital environments and expectations also shape attention and wellbeing.

prerequisites: Access to the core digital environment used in the local context.
Enough orientation or support to attempt routine tasks safely.
cross_element_dependencies: Progress is easier when Digital Communication, Collaboration and Participation is at least emerging alongside this element.

Progress is easier when Digital Learning and Development is at least emerging alongside this element.
entries.respondent_visibility: Only partly visible externally; the most reliable judgment combines observable traces with self-reflection about boundaries, risk and wellbeing.
progression_signals: Moves from one-off fixes to deliberate boundary-setting.
Aligns digital presence more clearly with role and values.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Manages presence, privacy, boundaries and digital habits deliberately across contexts.
observable_practices: Reviews profiles and privacy settings deliberately so that public traces, privacy and role expectations are better aligned.
Uses notification patterns to support sustainable work patterns, healthier boundaries and appropriate availability.
Treats community norms as an ongoing part of trustworthy participation rather than a one-off compliance task.
evidence_examples: A deliberate review of profiles and privacy settings with role-appropriate choices about visibility, privacy or tone.
A sustained routine in notification patterns that supports healthier availability and attention.
Evidence that community norms is being managed as an ongoing practice rather than as a one-off fix.

common_misconceptions.claim: Good privacy settings are enough to manage digital identity.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Tone, boundaries, visibility, reputation and role expectations matter too.

common_misconceptions.claim: Wellbeing is separate from digital practice.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Availability, platform habits and communication norms affect wellbeing directly.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Individual Framework
entries.capability_statement: Models and shapes healthy, trustworthy and context-aware digital norms for wider groups or communities.
observable_practices: Uses profiles and privacy settings to model clear, context-aware digital presence for other people.
Shapes notification patterns in ways that support care, inclusion and sustainable participation beyond personal habits alone.
Contributes to community norms by helping groups think well about trust, boundaries, risk and wellbeing.
evidence_examples: Shared guidance or modelling related to profiles and privacy settings that other people use or reference.
Group norms or a support approach using notification patterns to improve sustainable participation.
A reflective or advisory piece about community norms that helps others balance trust, care and risk.

common_misconceptions.claim: Role modelling means telling others to follow the rules.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Proficient practice shapes culture through care, explanation and context-sensitive guidance.

common_misconceptions.claim: The safest digital presence is minimal visibility everywhere.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Healthy identity management balances opportunity, trust and risk rather than disappearing.
